primary_meaning: The firmament most commonly symbolizes the created heavens as a visible witness to God’s glory, sovereignty, and ordering of creation.
primary_basis: Genesis 1:6–8, 14–18 — God creates and orders the firmament, naming it heaven and placing the heavenly lights within it.
Psalm 150:1 — God is praised in “the firmament of his power.”
Daniel 12:3 — the brightness of the firmament supplies an image for the glory of the righteous.

alternatives.meaning: The firmament is primarily a cosmological feature rather than a symbol: the expanse or dome separating the waters above from those below.
The firmament refers to the ordinary visible sky or atmosphere, including the region in which birds fly and weather occurs.
The firmament denotes heaven or the celestial realm and therefore represents divine transcendence, authority, or the boundary between earthly and heavenly realities.
The firmament represents separation, boundaries, and the establishment of order out of primordial chaos.
In some patristic and medieval allegories, the firmament signifies the Church, Scripture, spiritual knowledge, or steadfast believers who separate higher spiritual realities from lower earthly ones.
basis: Interpretive associations with the apostles, teachers, or saints as heavenly lights

notes: There is no settled, uniquely Christian symbolic meaning of “firmament.” Its basic biblical function is cosmological, while its most recognizable symbolic use—especially from Psalm 19:1—is as the created heavens bearing witness to God’s glory and ordered power. Interpretations also vary according to whether the underlying Hebrew raqia is understood as a solid vault, an expanse, the atmosphere, outer space, or heaven.
